title: He wept over it (Luke 19:41–44)
hook: Jesus weeps over Jerusalem: if thou hadst known the things for peace

segments.voice: Yesterday, ten servants with one pound each, and one who buried his in a napkin. Your line was trade with it.

On the western slope of the Mount of Olives there's a small church shaped like a teardrop. It was built in the 1950s, and its name is Latin: Dominus Flevit, the Lord wept. Behind the altar, a big window looks straight across the valley at the old city of Jerusalem, so the priest at Mass faces the view. On the front of the altar is a mosaic of a hen gathering her chicks. The church marks one moment. Jesus has come down the hill on a colt, with crowds shouting praise. And then, at the sight of the city, he stops.
screen: `A CHURCH SHAPED LIKE A TEAR.` → `DOMINUS FLEVIT: THE LORD WEPT.` → `A WINDOW FACING THE CITY.`

segments.voice: It's what Christians call Palm Sunday. Crowds are spreading their cloaks on the road, shouting blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord. In the middle of that joyful procession, Luke says: "And when he drew near, seeing the city, he wept over it." Luke's word means to weep aloud, to sob. Then he speaks to the city: "If thou also hadst known, and that in this thy day, the things that are to thy peace; but now they are hidden from thy eyes." There's a play on words in it. Many people heard the name Jerusalem as containing shalom, peace. The city of peace hasn't recognized what makes for peace. Then he grieves over what's coming: enemies will surround the city, and not leave a stone upon a stone, because thou hast not known the time of thy visitation. Christians later read these words in light of what happened about forty years after: in the year 70 the Roman army besieged Jerusalem and destroyed the Temple, and many thousands died. Hear it the way Jesus says it. He doesn't gloat. He doesn't curse. He weeps, the way you'd weep over a child running toward a road. Remember the hen: how often would I have gathered thy children. It's the same love. Catholics hear in this a God who isn't distant from the suffering of cities. Before the stones fall, someone stood on a hill and cried for them by name.
screen: `THE JOYFUL PROCESSION, THEN TEARS.` · `WEPT ALOUD, NOT A QUIET TEAR.` · `THE CITY OF PEACE MISSED PEACE.` · `GRIEF, NOT GLOATING.` · then, large: `THE THINGS THAT ARE TO THY PEACE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one city where people are living through war or violence, and picture it from a hill, the way Jesus saw Jerusalem: rooftops, a market, a hospital, children going somewhere. Let yourself feel something for the people there, without needing to fix it or take a side. If you pray, ask for the things that make for peace there; if you don't, hold them in your attention with care.
Visitation. The time Jerusalem didn't know, when Jesus looked at the city in the middle of a joyful procession and sobbed. Today's word.
Your line: the things for peace. Grief, not gloating, from the hill. Day four hundred seventy-seven, done.

howItsDone: Pilgrims in the Holy Land celebrate Mass at the Dominus Flevit chapel on the Mount of Olives, facing the old city, and Catholics pray for peace in Jerusalem and in places at war in the prayers of the faithful.

original.note: Greek: he wept aloud, sobbed. A stronger word than the quiet tears at Lazarus' tomb in John.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus was sad that people rejected him.
what it means: he grieves for the city itself and for what will happen to its people, because it didn't know what made for peace.
what a scholar hears: Luke uses eklausen, loud weeping; John 11:35 uses edakrusen, shed tears. Many heard shalom in the name Jerusalem.
recall: to give up whatever comes before him

chat.says: Why did Jesus cry when he saw Jerusalem, right in the middle of a happy parade?
options: He grieved that the city missed the things for its peace, and what was coming.
He was afraid of what would happen to him in the city that week.
He was angry at the crowds for shouting and wanted them to stop.
chat.meaning: Luke says he wept over the city because it hadn't known the things that are to its peace, nor the time of its visitation.

visitation.meaning: the time God came close to the city

notes: Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 19:41 and 19:42.
Dominus Flevit: built 1955 by Antonio Barluzzi in a teardrop shape, window facing the old city, hen-and-chicks mosaic on the altar front. Confirm details.
Year 70 siege: framed as Rome's action; Jesus' weeping as grief, not curse. Confirm the framing avoids any blame of Jewish people.
Folk etymology of Jerusalem with shalom: 'many heard' is used to avoid claiming a scientific etymology. Confirm.
